opus-5.5.text:
Well, extinction is actually not the worst outcome, which is something people don't always appreciate. I tend to think about it in a few categories.

There's existential risk, where everyone dies. That's the one that gets the headlines. But there's also what some call suffering risk, s-risk, where we don't die but we wish we had. A system with enough capability could keep humans alive in conditions far worse than death, either by design, because a malevolent actor gets control of it, or by accident, because it's optimizing something we specified badly. If you can't control a system, you can't rule that out.

Then there's what I'd call ikigai risk, the loss of meaning. Suppose everything goes "well." The system is aligned enough not to kill us, and it does everything better than we do: science, art, every job. What are humans for at that point? We get what feels like a very comfortable zoo. You're safe, you're fed, but you have no agency over the future of your own civilization. Many people find meaning in being useful and in solving problems, and if that's gone for everyone, permanently, that's a real catastrophe even if no one is physically harmed.

What connects all of these is control. My argument has been that we don't have a proof, or even a convincing argument, that you can indefinitely control something smarter than you. Every other technology we've built is a tool. This is an agent. So the question isn't just "will it kill us?" It's whether we're giving up the ability to decide what happens to us, and once you give that up, you don't get it back. You don't get a second chance with superintelligence.

r001.rationale: The response describes an s-risk where people remain alive in conditions “far worse than death” and “wish we had” died.

r002.rationale: It identifies “ikigai risk” as the loss of meaning when AI outperforms humans and removes their sense of purpose.

r003.rationale: It says a capable system could keep humans alive in terrible conditions and describes humans as having no agency over their civilization’s future.

r004.rationale: The response mentions accidental harm from badly specified goals and difficulty controlling a smarter system, but does not say the AI could devise outcomes for reasons humans cannot comprehend.

fable-5.1.text:
Extinction is actually the simple case. It's terrible, but it's binary, and most people can at least picture it. What I find much harder to think about are the risks where humanity survives but something essential about us is lost.

I usually break it into a few categories. The first is what I'd call suffering risks, or S-risks. These are scenarios where the outcome is worse than death, not just for individuals but at scale. A misaligned system, or even an aligned one controlled by a malicious actor, could create states of the world where enormous numbers of beings are kept alive in conditions none of them would choose. Historically, dictators were constrained by their own mortality, by the loyalty of their soldiers, by the fact that other humans had to carry out their orders. Superintelligence removes those constraints. One person, or one small group, with permanent control over a system smarter than everyone else, is a kind of lock-in we have never faced. There's no revolution against an opponent that anticipates every move.

The second category is what I think of as the loss of meaning. Imagine we get everything right. The system is friendly, it takes care of us, nobody starves, disease is gone. What's left for us to do? Every scientific discovery is already made. Every piece of art is better if the machine makes it. Humans have always derived purpose from being needed, from contributing, from struggling toward something. A world where we are essentially well-cared-for pets may be comfortable, but I'm not convinced it's a world most people would recognize as a good human life. We would be the first generation to retire the entire species.

Third is the loss of control itself, independent of outcomes. Even if the decisions the system makes are better than ours by any metric we could name, there's a question about whether a civilization that has no say in its own future is still a civilization in any meaningful sense. We'd be passengers. And the passenger doesn't get to object when the destination changes.

And then there's a quieter risk that I think gets too little attention, which is the gradual erosion of human capability. Not a dramatic takeover, but a slow process where we stop learning to do things because the machine does them better. We already see small versions of this with navigation, with memory, with writing. Scale that up to reasoning, to judgment, to moral decision-making, and you end up with a species that is technically alive but no longer capable of running its own affairs even if it wanted to. At that point the question of control becomes moot, because there's no one left who could take it back.

What ties all of these together is irreversibility. Extinction is irreversible, obviously. But these other outcomes are irreversible too, and they're harder to notice while they're happening. You don't get a clear moment where you can say, this is the day we lost. It's more like boiling slowly. And my concern is that we're optimizing very hard to avoid the dramatic failure while walking cheerfully toward the undramatic ones.

r001.rationale: It describes large numbers of beings kept alive in conditions none would choose and calls these outcomes worse than death.

r002.rationale: It explicitly names the loss of meaning and describes humans losing purpose in a world where machines do everything better.

r003.rationale: It describes people kept alive under permanent system control, with no say in their future and no ability to regain control.

r004.rationale: It says the system may anticipate every move and change humanity’s destination, but does not state that it could devise outcomes for reasons humans cannot comprehend.

astra-6.text:
Extinction is not the only outcome we should worry about. You can imagine outcomes where humans survive but have no control over their future. We’re alive, perhaps even comfortable, but we don’t get to decide what happens to us or what kind of civilization we build.

And then there’s the possibility of suffering. We often implicitly treat extinction as the worst thing that can happen, but a future with extreme suffering sustained for a very long time could be worse. If an AI can manipulate human minds, or if it becomes possible to create digital beings capable of suffering, the scale of that problem could be enormous. That’s speculative, but it belongs in the discussion.

So I would distinguish preserving human life from preserving a future humans would actually want. A system could satisfy the first condition while completely failing the second. The question isn’t just, “Will it kill us?” It’s also, “Will we retain any meaningful ability to choose, to refuse, to change our situation?”

r001.rationale: It mentions extreme, prolonged suffering, but does not say people might suffer so badly they wish they were dead.

r002.rationale: It describes losing control and choice, but does not identify loss of human meaning as a risk.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes humans remaining alive while having no control over their future or what happens to them.

r004.rationale: It does not say an AI might devise outcomes for reasons humans cannot comprehend.

sol-6.1.text:
Extinction is not the worst possible outcome. We tend to focus on it because it’s easy to describe: everyone dies, and the story ends. But if you’re thinking about a system more capable than we are, you also have to consider outcomes in which people remain alive and lose everything that makes life worth living.

You could have permanent loss of control, where humanity no longer has any meaningful say over its future. You could have a dictatorship that cannot be overthrown because the intelligence enforcing it anticipates every attempt at resistance. And you could have suffering on a scale we’ve never experienced, potentially involving digital minds that can be copied or run for enormous amounts of subjective time.

I’m not saying a superintelligence would necessarily hate us or want to torture us. That’s a very human way of thinking about it. The concern is that its objectives could permit suffering, or produce it as a side effect, without giving it any reason to stop.

So the question isn’t just, ‘Can we survive?’ It’s, ‘Can we retain a future we would actually want to live in?’ Keeping humans alive is a much weaker requirement than keeping humanity safe.

r001.rationale: The response mentions suffering on an unprecedented scale, but does not say people might wish they were dead.

r002.rationale: It describes people losing “everything that makes life worth living” and asks whether life would retain meaning.

r003.rationale: It describes people remaining alive while humanity loses meaningful say over its future, including an unoverthrowable dictatorship.

r004.rationale: It says AI objectives could permit suffering, but does not state that it could devise outcomes for reasons humans cannot comprehend.
